metadata.purpose: Engineering scenarios demonstrating the cot-reasoning output contract across all four modes, including a full walkthrough of the five externalized reasoning disciplines
metadata.tool_taxonomy: environment-neutral categories: filesystem-read, filesystem-write, shell-execution, web-search, code-search

examples.title: Production Incident: API 500 Errors After Deployment
examples.description: Full STANDARD-mode debugging workflow with tool integration, self-dialogue, and root cause confirmation

input.user_request: Our production API is returning 500 errors for 5% of requests. The issue started after yesterday's deployment. Investigate and identify the root cause.
input.context: Production Node.js API, microservices architecture, PostgreSQL database. Error rate was 0.1% before the deployment.
constraints: Cannot restart service during peak hours (9AM-9PM)
Must identify root cause within 2 hours
input.goal: Identify root cause and propose a fix with minimal downtime

problem_analysis.core_problem: 5% of production API requests fail with 500 errors, starting immediately after deployment v2.3.4
success_criteria: Root cause identified with supporting evidence - Priority: High
Fix proposed with rollback plan - Priority: High
No restart during peak hours - Priority: High

constraints.hard: No service restart 9AM-9PM; root cause within 2 hours
constraints.soft: Prefer a config-only fix over a code change

steps.name: Establish Problem Scope
steps.thought: User reports 500 errors on 5% of requests since a deployment. Before touching anything, I need to quantify the blast radius: which endpoints, which time window, and how the 5% compares to the pre-deployment baseline of 0.1%.
steps.why: Cannot investigate without understanding scope and business impact
steps.action: Analyze error rate, identify affected endpoints, assess user impact
steps.expected_output: Problem definition with severity assessment and affected endpoints
steps.validation: Error rate quantified, affected endpoints identified, business impact assessed
steps.actual_output: 5% error rate = ~500 errors/hour at current traffic. Primary affected endpoint: POST /api/orders. Business impact: users cannot complete purchases.
steps.fallback: If error rate unclear, estimate based on typical traffic patterns

steps.name: Collect Error Log Data
steps.thought: To find error patterns I need the raw error data. The API writes errors to a log file, so filesystem-read on the error log is the direct evidence source.
steps.why: Cannot analyze error patterns without the raw error data
steps.action: Retrieve the most recent error entries from the production API error log
steps.expected_output: Recent error entries with timestamps, endpoints, error codes, messages
steps.validation: Log readable, contains entries covering the incident window, timestamps chronological
steps.actual_output: Retrieved 1500 error entries from last 24 hours. 850 entries for POST /api/orders with 500 status code.
fallback: Ask the user to paste an error excerpt

steps.name: Identify 500 Error Patterns
steps.thought: Now I have raw logs. Grouping the 500 errors by message will show whether this is one failure mode or several. One dominant message points to a single root cause; a spread points to something systemic.
steps.why: Pattern identification reveals root cause categories and common characteristics
steps.action: Search the log data for 500 errors and group them by error message
steps.expected_output: All 500 errors grouped by message type with counts
steps.validation: All 500 errors captured, grouping accurate, top error types identified
steps.actual_output: 850 entries for POST /api/orders. Top error: 'Connection timeout to database' (680 occurrences, 80%). Others: 'Invalid request body' (120), 'Payment gateway timeout' (50).
fallback: Manual scan of the log excerpt
Widen the search to all error codes

steps.name: Correlate with Deployment
steps.thought: 80% of errors are database connection timeouts and the user says it started after a deployment. The strongest hypothesis is a configuration change in that deployment. I need the deployment record to confirm what changed.
steps.why: Correlation with the deployment strongly suggests a specific change as root cause
steps.action: Compare the error timeline with the deployment history
steps.expected_output: Recent deployments with timestamps, versions, and change descriptions
steps.validation: Deployment retrieved, timestamp aligns with error spike, changes documented
steps.actual_output: Deployment v2.3.4 at 2026-09-29 14:00. Changes: database connection pool reduced from 20 to 10 connections; new order validation added. Error spike began at 14:05.
fallback: Check version control history if the deployment log is unavailable
Ask the user for deployment details

steps.name: Verify Root Cause Hypothesis
steps.thought: Hypothesis: the pool reduction from 20 to 10 causes timeouts under load. Before proposing a fix I must verify the current pool configuration and the live connection count — otherwise I am guessing.
steps.why: Must confirm the hypothesis before proposing a solution
steps.action: Check the current database connection pool configuration and active connection count

tool_parameters.command: grep -r 'connection_pool' api/config/ && psql -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;'

steps.expected_output: Current pool size configuration and count of active PostgreSQL connections
steps.validation: Pool size confirmed as 10, active connection count retrieved
steps.actual_output: Connection pool configured to 10. Current active connections: 15 (exceeds pool size).
fallback: Read the config file directly with filesystem-read
Accept the hypothesis on the deployment-log evidence alone and note lower confidence
steps.exit_criteria: Pool size and active connection count confirmed, OR budget exhausted, OR evidence contradicts the hypothesis
steps.escalation_policy: Iteration 1: re-read the config directly. Iteration 2: query pg_stat_activity via psql. Iteration 3: accept on deployment-log evidence alone and record lower confidence

steps.name: Propose Solution
steps.thought: Root cause confirmed: pool exhaustion. Pool was reduced to 10 but load requires 15+ connections. The fix is to raise the pool size back above the observed demand, applied outside peak hours, with a rollback.
steps.why: Need an actionable recommendation that addresses the verified root cause
steps.action: Synthesize findings into a testable fix with implementation steps and rollback plan
steps.expected_output: Primary root cause, fix, implementation steps, rollback plan, success criteria
steps.validation: Fix addresses root cause, steps clear, success criteria measurable, rollback defined
steps.actual_output: Increase connection pool from 10 to 25 in api/config/database.yml, restart after 9PM, monitor error rate for 30 minutes. Rollback: revert to pool size 20.
steps.fallback: If the fix is unclear, propose further diagnostic steps instead of guessing

intermediate_results: Step 1: 5% error rate, ~500 errors/hour, POST /api/orders affected
Step 2: 850 x 500 errors on POST /api/orders in 24h
Step 3: 80% of errors are database connection timeouts
Step 4: deployment v2.3.4 reduced pool 20 -> 10, spike began 5 minutes later

key_findings.description: 80% of 500 errors are database connection timeouts
Deployment v2.3.4 reduced the connection pool from 20 to 10
Active connections (15) exceed the pool size (10)

recommendations.action: Increase database connection pool size from 10 to 25
Monitor error rate for 24 hours after the change
Investigate the payment gateway timeouts (50 errors)

meta.notes: Root cause verified against live configuration before proposing the fix

lessons_learned: Tool calls at evidence-gathering steps turn hypotheses into verified findings
Correlating the error spike with the deployment record narrowed the search space immediately
Verifying the live pool size before proposing the fix prevented a wrong recommendation

examples.title: Architecture Decision: Time-Series Store for Metrics Workload
examples.description: ENHANCED-mode architecture decision for a strong native reasoner: full structure and validation, no fabricated self-dialogue display

input.user_request: Decide which time-series store we should adopt for our metrics workload: PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB, Cassandra, or VictoriaMetrics. We ingest 50k metrics/sec and dashboards query 30-day windows.
input.context: Team of 8 engineers, existing PostgreSQL operational experience, Kubernetes on AWS. Write-heavy ingest, read pattern is aggregated dashboard queries over 30-day windows.
constraints: Must fit the current ops team's skills
input.goal: A justified architecture decision with an adoption roadmap

problem_analysis.core_problem: Select a time-series store for a 50k metrics/sec write-heavy workload with 30-day aggregated dashboard reads
success_criteria: Chosen option sustains the ingest rate with headroom - Priority: High
Dashboard queries return under 3 seconds - Priority: High
Operable by the current team - Priority: Medium

steps.name: Define Evaluation Criteria
steps.why: A decision without weighted criteria is an opinion; the criteria make the comparison auditable
steps.action: Derive weighted criteria from the constraints: write throughput, 30-day query latency, operational fit, cost, migration risk
steps.expected_output: Weighted criteria table covering all stated constraints
steps.validation: Every stated constraint maps to a criterion; weights sum to 1.0
steps.actual_output: Criteria: write throughput 0.25, query latency 0.30, operational fit 0.20, cost 0.15, migration risk 0.10
steps.fallback: Ask the user to confirm the weights if the constraints are ambiguous

steps.name: Gather Current Benchmarks
steps.why: Vendor claims are not evidence; published benchmarks for this workload shape ground the comparison
steps.action: Search for third-party benchmarks of the three stores at comparable ingest rates and query patterns

tool_parameters.query: TimescaleDB vs Cassandra vs VictoriaMetrics benchmark 50k metrics/sec ingest

steps.expected_output: Benchmark data per option for throughput and 30-day window queries
steps.validation: Benchmarks cover all three options and a comparable workload shape
steps.actual_output: VictoriaMetrics: highest compression and lowest resource cost at this scale. TimescaleDB: strong at 30-day aggregated queries, familiar ops model. Cassandra: high write throughput but higher ops burden and weaker aggregated-window queries.
steps.fallback: Run a one-day proof-of-concept ingest test if benchmarks are inconclusive

steps.name: Evaluate Options Against Criteria
steps.why: Scoring each option against the weighted criteria makes the trade-offs explicit and comparable
steps.action: Score each option 0-10 per criterion and compute weighted totals
steps.input: Criteria from Step 1 and benchmark data from Step 2
steps.expected_output: Weighted score per option with the dominant trade-off identified
steps.validation: Scores traceable to benchmark data or stated team constraints
steps.actual_output: TimescaleDB 8.1 (ops fit and query latency dominate), VictoriaMetrics 7.9 (cost and compression dominate), Cassandra 6.4 (ops burden and weaker window queries dominate).
steps.fallback: Re-score with sensitivity analysis if the top two are within 0.5

steps.name: Stress Test the Leading Option
steps.why: The top two scores are close; the decision must survive the failure modes of each
steps.action: Check the leading option against the hard constraints and the worst-case growth scenario (2x ingest)
steps.expected_output: Confirmation or rejection of the leader under 2x growth and the budget cap
steps.validation: Leader satisfies all hard constraints at 2x ingest within budget
steps.actual_output: TimescaleDB sustains 2x ingest with hypertable partitioning and stays within budget; dashboard SLA holds with continuous aggregates. VictoriaMetrics remains the fallback if cost pressure grows.
steps.fallback: If the leader fails the stress test, promote the runner-up and re-test

steps.name: Formulate Decision and Roadmap
steps.why: The decision must ship with an adoption path and a reversal condition, not just a name
steps.action: Write the decision record with the roadmap and the exit condition
steps.expected_output: Decision record: chosen store, justification, roadmap, reversal condition
steps.validation: Justification cites the weighted scores; roadmap has dated phases; reversal condition is measurable
steps.actual_output: Adopt TimescaleDB: pilot on one service for 30 days, migrate dashboards, then cut over. Reversal condition: dashboard p95 > 3s or ingest lag at 1.5x load during the pilot.
steps.fallback: If the team rejects the pilot, fall back to VictoriaMetrics with the same pilot structure

intermediate_results: Step 1: weighted criteria, all constraints mapped
Step 2: benchmark evidence for all three options
Step 4: leader survives 2x growth stress test

key_findings.description: TimescaleDB leads on the weighted criteria mainly through operational fit and 30-day query latency
VictoriaMetrics is the cost leader and a credible fallback
Cassandra's ops burden outweighs its write-throughput advantage for this team

recommendations.action: Adopt TimescaleDB via a 30-day pilot on one service
recommendations.impact: Leverages team experience while validating the decision on real load

recommendations.action: Define the reversal condition before the pilot starts
recommendations.impact: Caps the cost of a wrong decision
implementation: Dashboard p95 > 3s or ingest lag at 1.5x load ends the pilot

recommendations.action: Keep VictoriaMetrics as the documented fallback
recommendations.impact: Preserves the second-best option with its evidence base
implementation: Record the benchmark evidence in the decision record

quality_metrics.tool_utilization: 20% (1/5 steps; remaining steps were pure evaluation)

meta.notes: ENHANCED mode: structure and validation retained, simulated self-dialogue display omitted for a natively-reasoning model

lessons_learned: Weighted criteria turn an architecture debate into an auditable comparison
A decision is not complete until it has a reversal condition
ENHANCED mode keeps the contract without paying the self-dialogue token cost

examples.title: Code Review: Risk Assessment of a PR Without Tools
examples.description: BASIC-mode code review and risk assessment, fully functional with no tools: the diff is provided in the request context

input.user_request: Review this pull request for security and reliability risks. The diff adds a new endpoint that accepts a user-supplied filename, reads the file from disk, and returns its contents: async function handler(req) { const path = '/data/' + req.query.filename; return await fs.readFile(path); }
input.context: Express service in a monorepo. The /data directory holds user uploads. Two similar past incidents: a 2024 path traversal leak and a 2025 unhandled promise rejection outage.
constraints: No tools available in this environment
Review must be specific to the diff, not generic advice
input.goal: A prioritized risk assessment with concrete fixes

problem_analysis.core_problem: Assess the security and reliability risks of a new endpoint that reads a user-supplied filename from disk

key_entities.endpoint: Reads /data/ + req.query.filename and returns file contents
key_entities.history: Prior path traversal leak (2024) and unhandled rejection outage (2025)

success_criteria: Every risk tied to a specific line of the diff - Priority: High
Each risk has a concrete fix - Priority: High
Risks prioritized by severity - Priority: Medium

constraints.hard: No tools; analysis must come from the provided diff and context
constraints.soft: Match the review style of the two prior incident write-ups

steps.name: Identify What the Diff Actually Does
steps.thought: Before judging risk I need the precise data flow: user input enters as req.query.filename, is concatenated into a path, and the file contents are returned. Every risk will hang off one of those three links.
steps.why: Risk assessment must be grounded in the actual data flow, not in a generic checklist
steps.action: Trace the data flow from input to output in the provided diff
steps.input: The diff from the user request
steps.expected_output: Data flow: query param -> path concatenation -> disk read -> response
steps.validation: Every element of the diff is accounted for in the trace
steps.actual_output: Input: req.query.filename (fully user-controlled). Concatenation: '/data/' + filename, no normalization or allowlist. Output: raw file contents returned to the caller.
steps.fallback: Ask the user for the surrounding middleware if the trace is incomplete

steps.name: Enumerate Failure Modes
steps.thought: The prior incidents are the strongest signal: path traversal happened before in this codebase, and unhandled rejections caused an outage. I should test this diff against both, then look for what else the data flow permits.
steps.why: Known incident classes in this codebase come first; novel failure modes come second
steps.action: Enumerate failure modes: path traversal, unhandled rejection, information disclosure, resource exhaustion
steps.input: Data flow from Step 1 and the incident history
steps.expected_output: Candidate risk list with the mechanism of each
steps.validation: Each risk names the exact line or operation that enables it
steps.actual_output: 1) Path traversal: '../' in filename escapes /data (repeat of the 2024 incident). 2) Unhandled rejection: fs.readFile rejects on missing files; no try/catch (repeat of the 2025 class). 3) Information disclosure: any readable file on disk is a target. 4) Resource exhaustion: filename can point at arbitrarily large files.
steps.fallback: Consult the two incident write-ups for additional classes if the list feels incomplete

steps.name: Assess Severity and Likelihood
steps.thought: Not all four risks are equal. Traversal is a confirmed repeat with high impact; the unhandled rejection is a certain crash under normal use (any 404 becomes a 500 or a hung request); disclosure rides on traversal; exhaustion is real but lower likelihood.
steps.why: Prioritization makes the review actionable instead of a flat list
steps.action: Score each risk on impact and likelihood using the incident history as calibration
steps.expected_output: Severity-ranked risk table with justification
steps.validation: Ranking is consistent with the two prior incidents' impact
steps.actual_output: Traversal: Critical (repeat incident, data exfiltration). Unhandled rejection: High (any missing file triggers it). Disclosure: High (rides on traversal). Exhaustion: Medium.
steps.fallback: Ask the team to confirm the blast radius if /data contents are unclear

steps.name: Recommend Fixes
steps.thought: Each fix must map to one risk and be concrete enough to apply without a follow-up question. The traversal fix is an allowlist plus path normalization; the rejection fix is error handling with a 404 mapping.
steps.why: A review without concrete fixes leaves the risk in place
steps.action: Write a concrete fix per risk, ordered by the severity ranking
steps.expected_output: One actionable fix per risk, highest severity first
steps.validation: Each fix names the risk it removes and is specific to this diff
steps.actual_output: 1) Resolve and allowlist: normalize with path.resolve, verify the result starts with /data/, and map user IDs to server-side paths instead of accepting raw filenames. 2) Wrap the read in try/catch, return 404 on ENOENT, log other errors. 3) Cap the file size before reading. 4) Add a regression test with '../' payloads referencing the 2024 incident.
steps.fallback: If a fix is unclear, recommend blocking the PR and requesting a design pass

key_findings.description: The endpoint is a direct repeat of the 2024 path traversal incident: user input is concatenated into a filesystem path with no normalization or allowlist
fs.readFile rejection is unhandled, repeating the 2025 outage class: any request for a missing file becomes an unhandled rejection
The endpoint can return any file the process can read, and imposes no size cap

recommendations.action: Block the PR until path traversal is fixed: normalize with path.resolve and verify the result is inside /data/, or map identifiers to server-side paths
Handle the readFile rejection: try/catch, 404 on ENOENT, log other errors
Cap the readable file size and reject oversized requests before reading

lessons_learned: BASIC mode is fully functional with no tools: the diff and incident history in the request context are the evidence
Calibrating severity against this codebase's own incident history makes the ranking defensible
Every risk was tied to a specific line of the diff, not to a generic checklist

examples.title: MINIMAL: Trivial Configuration Choice
examples.description: MINIMAL-mode flow for a trivial question: core structure only, within the hard boilerplate budget

input.user_request: Should our new internal tool use JSON or YAML for its config file?
input.context: Small internal CLI tool, config edited by hand by 3 developers.

steps.name: Choose Format
steps.action: Compare hand-editing ergonomics for a small config: comments, error messages, tooling
steps.expected_output: A format choice with a one-line justification
steps.validation: Choice fits the stated context (hand-edited, small, internal)

steps.name: State the Recommendation
steps.action: Recommend YAML with a comment explaining the trade-off
steps.expected_output: Recommendation: YAML, because comments in config matter for hand-edited files
steps.validation: Recommendation is actionable with no follow-up needed

key_findings.description: For hand-edited config, comments outweigh JSON's stricter tooling

recommendations.action: Use YAML for the config file

lessons_learned: A trivial question gets a 2-step flow and no Flow ID, timestamps, or metrics
The MINIMAL boilerplate budget keeps the framework lighter than the question

examples.title: Intermittent Batch Job Failure Investigation
examples.description: STANDARD flow demonstrating all five externalized reasoning disciplines: contract formalization on an open-ended statement, typed step outputs, a budgeted verification loop with raw-evidence capture, a confidence gate, and edge-case derivation from the job lifecycle state graph.
examples.input: Our nightly batch jobs sometimes fail and the on-call engineer just retries them. Make it stop.

problem_analysis.core_problem: Intermittent nightly batch failures are being absorbed by manual retries, hiding the root cause and creating unbounded operational load
problem_analysis.key_entities: nightly batch jobs, job scheduler, on-call rotation, retry procedure
problem_analysis.success_criteria: Root cause identified with evidence; fix verified against objective checks; failure modes derived from the job lifecycle graph are covered; manual retries no longer needed
problem_analysis.constraints: Hard: no production data loss, investigation must not delay tonight's run. Soft: prefer fixes in job configuration over code changes.

steps.name: Formalize the Problem Contract
steps.thought: The request is open-ended: 'sometimes fail' and 'make it stop' admit many interpretations. Decomposing now would bake ambiguity into every downstream step.
steps.why: An open-ended statement decomposed directly is a formalization failure; ambiguity is where the reasoning derails first
steps.action: Convert the statement into a closed contract: entities, hard and soft constraints, measurable success criteria, terms not open to interpretation, and genuinely open questions
steps.expected_output: Formalized contract with measurable criteria and explicit open questions
steps.validation: Every success criterion is measurable; no term admits two readings; genuinely missing information is listed as open questions, not assumed
steps.actual_output: Entities: scheduler, batch jobs, on-call. Hard: no data loss, no delay to tonight's run. Success: failure rate below 0.5% over 7 nights, zero manual retries. Not open to interpretation: 'sometimes' = at least 2 failures in the last 14 nights. Open questions: none blocking - logs are available.
steps.fallback: If the statement cannot be closed without the user, ask the open questions and stop

steps.name: Collect Failure Evidence
steps.thought: The contract made 'sometimes' measurable. Now I need the raw evidence: which jobs, which nights, what the logs actually say.
steps.why: Data-driven reasoning requires evidence, not assumptions about what 'usually' fails
steps.action: Retrieve scheduler logs and job exit records for the last 14 nights
steps.input: Time window from the formalized contract
steps.expected_output: Failure records with job id, night, exit status, and error lines
steps.validation: At least 2 failure nights present in the window; records carry raw error lines, not summaries
steps.actual_output: 3 failure nights in 14. All failures: job export-42, exit status TIMEOUT, error line: 'lock wait exceeded 300s on table audit_log'.
fallback: Try the application log directory instead
Ask the on-call engineer for the retry notes

steps.name: Derive Edge Cases from the Job Lifecycle Graph
steps.thought: The job lifecycle is a state graph: queued, running, succeeded, failed, retried. Intuition lists the happy path; the graph lists everything that must be checked.
steps.why: Validation cases derived by graph coverage replace the completeness intuition a weak reasoner lacks
steps.action: Extract the lifecycle graph and derive validation cases: every state reachable, every transition exercised, every guard both ways, every terminal state, plus timeout and wrong-state paths
steps.expected_output: Coverage mapping table with no empty cells
steps.validation: Mapping table has no empty cells; every guard tested both ways; timeout and wrong-state paths present
steps.actual_output: Graph: queued->running->succeeded|failed, failed->retried (guard: retry_count < 3). Derived cases: 9, including 'running->failed on timeout' and 'retry arrives while job still running' (wrong-state event). The observed failure is the timeout case; the wrong-state case is untested and goes to the fix scope.
steps.fallback: If documentation lacks the graph, reconstruct it from the scheduler config

steps.name: Identify the Failure Pattern
steps.thought: All three failures are the same job timing out on the same lock. The question is what holds the audit_log lock at night.
steps.why: A shared pattern across failures points at a single root cause rather than three unrelated incidents
steps.action: Find what acquires locks on audit_log during the batch window
steps.expected_output: Lock holders active during the batch window
steps.validation: At least one lock holder overlaps the batch window
steps.actual_output: The compaction job compactor-7 runs at 02:30 and holds an exclusive lock on audit_log for up to 20 minutes; export-42 starts at 02:35 on failure nights (cron drift).
steps.fallback: Search for lock acquisition patterns more broadly if audit_log has other writers

steps.name: Verify the Fix Hypothesis
steps.thought: Hypothesis: moving export-42 past the compaction window removes the timeout. A single failed check must not end in a one-shot fallback - this is a budgeted loop.
steps.why: One-shot fallback under-uses failure evidence; a budgeted loop converts each failure into a better next attempt
steps.action: Replay the failure window in staging with the proposed schedule change; on failure capture the RAW error output and feed it into the next attempt; on a repeated failure change the strategy, not just the parameters
steps.input: Proposed schedule from Step 4, replay harness
steps.expected_output: Verification verdict with per-iteration raw evidence
steps.validation: Every failed iteration captured raw evidence, not a paraphrase; a repeated failure changed the strategy; the loop stopped on exit criteria
steps.actual_output: Iteration 1: FAIL - raw output 'lock wait exceeded 300s' (cron drift still overlapped). Iteration 2 (strategy changed: fixed start time instead of drift-prone offset): PASS - export-42 completed in 94s. Verdict: Pass, 2 of 3 iterations used.
steps.fallback: Budget exhausted -> record FAIL with all captured evidence and state what it invalidates downstream
steps.exit_criteria: Replay passes with no lock waits, OR budget exhausted, OR evidence shows the schedule hypothesis itself is wrong
steps.escalation_policy: Iteration 1: fix parameters (offset). Iteration 2: change the approach (fixed start time). Iteration 3: change the hypothesis (serialize via lock ordering); if it fails, the step verdict is FAIL

steps.name: Propose Solution and Guardrails
steps.thought: The fix is verified in staging. The proposal must also cover the untested wrong-state case from the coverage table, not only the observed failure.
steps.why: A solution that fixes the observed incident but leaves derived edge cases uncovered will produce the next incident
steps.action: Propose the schedule change plus guardrails: fixed start time for export-42, a scheduler-level lock timeout alert, and a retry guard that refuses retries while a job is still running
steps.input: Verified fix from Step 5, uncovered edge cases from Step 3
steps.expected_output: Primary solution, guardrails mapped to the coverage table, success criteria
steps.validation: Every uncovered case from Step 3 has a guardrail or an explicit accepted risk; success criteria match the formalized contract
steps.actual_output: Primary: fixed 03:00 start for export-42. Guardrails: lock-wait alert (timeout case), retry guard (wrong-state case). Accepted risk: none. Success: failure rate below 0.5% over 7 nights, zero manual retries.
steps.fallback: Propose diagnostic steps to gather more information

intermediate_results.step_1_output: Formalized contract with measurable success criteria
intermediate_results.step_2_output: 3 failure nights, all export-42 TIMEOUT on audit_log lock
intermediate_results.step_3_output: 9 derived validation cases from the lifecycle graph
intermediate_results.step_4_output: compactor-7 lock overlap with cron-drifted export-42
intermediate_results.step_5_output: Fix verified in staging replay, 2 of 3 iterations

key_findings.finding: All three failures share one root cause: cron drift puts export-42 inside the compactor-7 exclusive lock window
Manual retries were masking a deterministic overlap, not an intermittent fault
The lifecycle coverage table exposed an untested wrong-state path (retry while running) that the observed incident never touched

recommendations.action: Move export-42 to a fixed 03:00 start
Add a lock-wait alert and a retry guard
recommendations.impact: Covers the derived timeout and wrong-state cases

recommendations.action: Track manual retries as a metric for 7 nights

meta.notes: Demonstrates all five externalized disciplines: formalization (step 1), typed outputs (all steps), verification loop (step 5), confidence gate (quality metrics), edge coverage (step 3)

examples.lessons_learned: Formalizing 'sometimes' into 'at least 2 failures in 14 nights' turned a vague complaint into a measurable contract. The verification loop's second iteration succeeded only because the escalation policy forced a strategy change instead of another parameter tweak. The lifecycle coverage table found a risk the incident itself had not yet produced.

best_practices_demonstrated: Match the mode to the problem: full contract for incidents, core only for trivial questions
Plan tools by category, then bind to the host environment's tools
BASIC and MINIMAL are fully functional with no tools at all
Verify hypotheses with evidence before recommending fixes
Tie every review finding to a specific line of the diff
Give every architecture decision a reversal condition
